analysis.one_liner: Bars medical debt from appearing on credit reports and from being used in lending decisions.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by six Senate Democrats and referred to the Banking Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill amends the Fair Credit Reporting Act so that medical debt — including medical bills sent to collections — can no longer appear on a person's credit report [S2]. It also requires the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to write rules within a year barring creditors from considering medical debt when deciding whether to lend [S2]. Right now, an unpaid hospital bill can drop a credit score sharply and follow someone for years, affecting their ability to rent an apartment, buy a car, or get a mortgage. The bill would cut that link, though it would not erase the underlying debt.
analysis.who_benefits: The millions of Americans who carry medical debt on their credit reports. Removing it can raise credit scores, which affects whether someone qualifies for a mortgage, car loan, apartment lease, or credit card, and at what interest rate. People whose only blemish is a medical bill — often from an emergency they did not choose — benefit most, because once the medical debt is excluded they may look like ordinary, creditworthy borrowers again [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with medical bills on their credit reports

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Fair Credit Reporting Act to exclude 'any adverse information related to a medical debt, including a medical debt that was placed for collection, charged to profit or loss, or subjected to any similar action' from consumer reports [S2].
It defines medical debt broadly — any debt tied to receiving medical services, products, or devices — so a hospital bill, an ambulance charge, or a dental balance all fall under the exclusion [S2].

It orders the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to amend its rules within one year so creditors are prohibited from obtaining or using medical debt information when deciding whether to extend credit [S2].

It removes the existing exceptions that currently allow credit reporting agencies to disclose medical information and medical contact information in limited circumstances, closing those loopholes [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Debt collection agencies and debt buyers would lose one of their main levers for pressuring people to pay medical bills: the threat of a damaged credit score [S2]. Credit reporting agencies and lenders that rely on medical debt data in underwriting would lose access to that information [S2]. Some lenders argue that medical debt helps predict repayment risk, so excluding it could, in their view, lead to tighter underwriting or slightly higher prices for some borrowers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Collection agencies, debt buyers, and credit bureaus

drawbacks.text: The bill does not erase medical debt or lower it — people would still owe the money and could still face calls and lawsuits from collectors; it only hides the debt from credit reports and lender decisions [S2].

Lenders argue medical debt carries information about repayment behavior, so removing it from underwriting could lead some to price all borrowers similarly, which critics say could mean higher rates or less credit for some applicants [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete for a large group: people who were financially healthy before an illness or injury stop being penalized on their credit reports for medical bills [S2]. The costs fall on collection firms, debt buyers, and credit bureaus that profit from medical debt data, and on lenders that lose one underwriting input [S2]. The honest limitation is that the bill treats the symptom — the credit score hit — not the underlying medical billing and debt problem, which it leaves untouched [S2].

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which has taken no action on it; the bill is sitting in committee while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced the Medical Debt Relief Act of 2025 on July 29, 2025, joined by five Democratic cosponsors: Sens. Blumenthal, Fetterman, Welch, Warnock, and Gillibrand [S1][S3].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs on the day it was introduced [S4].
The full action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral [S4].
All six senators who sponsor or cosponsor the bill are Democrats; no Republican has signed on [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has had to change anything: debt collectors, debt buyers, and credit reporting agencies keep operating under the current rules, and the tens of millions of people with medical debt on their credit reports keep carrying that penalty. The outcome is simply that the bill has not moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Debt collectors and credit bureaus, for now

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to strip medical debt from credit reports and bar its use in lending decisions.

for.name: 5 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.role: Original cosponsors (Blumenthal, Fetterman, Welch, Warnock, Gillibrand)

sides.party_line_note: No vote has occurred, so there is no roll-call to measure; all six supporters are Democrats and the bill sits in a Republican-controlled committee, but no one has spoken against it on the record.

industries.industry: Debt collection and medical debt buying
industries.note: These firms buy unpaid medical bills for pennies and profit by collecting from patients; credit reporting is one of their main tools for pressuring payment. The bill removes that tool by banning medical debt from consumer reports [S2].

The bureaus would lose medical debt as reportable data, reducing the information they sell to lenders [S2]. Some bureaus have already voluntarily limited medical collections reporting, so the marginal loss may be modest.

Lenders would be barred from considering medical debt in credit decisions, losing one underwriting input [S2]. Some argue this removes useful risk information; others note studies show medical debt is a weak predictor of repayment.

Providers lose credit reporting as a lever to collect from patients, which could increase uncompensated care pressure; at the same time, patients who keep their credit intact may be more able to pay other bills and access care.

analysis.trajectory: With six sponsors, no Republican cosponsors, and no action from the Banking Committee since the July 2025 referral, the bill is unlikely to advance this Congress; most bills referred to committee without a scheduled markup never reach the floor, and this one would probably expire when the 119th Congress ends unless leadership elevates it.
